content: Epilepsy is a prevalent neurological condition, and a significant proportion of individuals with epilepsy are resistant to standard drug treatments. These patients often require additional antiepileptic medications to manage their condition. Carisbamate is an orally administered drug that works by inhibiting voltage-gated sodium channels, and it has been proposed as a potential treatment for drug-resistant focal epilepsy. The primary objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and tolerability of carisbamate when used as an add-on therapy for individuals with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web) and MEDLINE, was conducted up to April 8, 2021. The search also included ongoing trial registries, reference lists, and direct communication with trial authors. The review focused on double-blind randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared carisbamate with either a placebo or another antiepileptic drug. Both parallel-group and cross-over study designs were eligible for inclusion. Two independent reviewers selected studies, assessed their quality, and extracted data. The primary outcome of interest was the proportion of participants achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency (responder rate). Secondary outcomes included seizure freedom, treatment withdrawal (for any reason or due to adverse events), adverse events, and quality of life. Data were analyzed using the Mantel-Haenszel statistical method, and results were presented as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The review included four RCTs with a total of 2,211 participants. All studies compared carisbamate to placebo in individuals with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Participants were all over 16 years of age and were concurrently taking at least one other antiepileptic drug. The included trials exhibited significant risk of bias, particularly due to high rates of treatment withdrawal and incomplete reporting of attrition. Additionally, the risk of detection bias was unclear, as none of the studies specified whether outcome assessors were blinded. Meta-analysis indicated that carisbamate was associated with a higher responder rate compared to placebo (RR 1.36, 95% CI 1.14 to 1.62; moderate-certainty evidence). A single study suggested that more participants in the carisbamate group achieved seizure freedom (RR 2.43, 95% CI 0.84 to 7.03), but the certainty of this evidence was very low. Similarly, more participants in the carisbamate group withdrew from treatment for any reason (RR 1.32, 95% CI 0.82 to 2.12) or due to adverse events (RR 1.80, 95% CI 0.78 to 4.17), but the evidence for these outcomes was also of very low certainty. There was no significant difference between the carisbamate and placebo groups in the proportion of participants experiencing at least one adverse event (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.30; low-certainty evidence). However, dizziness (RR 2.06, 95% CI 1.23 to 3.44; very low-certainty evidence) and somnolence (RR 1.82, 95% CI 1.28 to 2.58; low-certainty evidence) were more commonly reported in the carisbamate group. No significant differences were observed for fatigue (RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.68), headache (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.38), or nausea (RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.75). None of the included trials reported on quality of life outcomes. The authors concluded that carisbamate may have potential as an add-on therapy for drug-resistant focal epilepsy, as it demonstrated some efficacy and tolerability. However, the evidence for all outcomes except the responder rate was of low to very low certainty, making the reliability of these findings uncertain. The significant risk of bias in the included studies, along with statistical heterogeneity for some outcomes, further limits the applicability of these results to clinical practice. Additionally, the studies were of short duration and only included adult participants. Future research should focus on conducting well-designed RCTs with longer follow-up periods, a broader range of participants, and more comprehensive clinical outcomes, including different seizure types and quality of life measures.
